sections.content: Tulsa, Oklahoma doesn't always make the national headlines the way Phoenix or Dallas does. But experienced investors who know where to look are quietly building wealth here — and for good reason. Low entry prices, strong rental demand, and a diversifying economy make real estate deals in Tulsa OK some of the most accessible and profitable opportunities in the country right now. Whether you're a first-time wholesaler or a seasoned flipper looking to expand your portfolio, Tulsa deserves a serious look. If you're just getting started, check out our guide to [Real Estate Investing for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) for the foundational knowledge you'll need before diving into any market.
Tulsa Real Estate Market Overview

Tulsa is Oklahoma's second-largest city with a population of around 420,000 people and a metro area approaching 1 million. The city has historically relied on energy, aerospace, and manufacturing, but recent years have brought significant diversification. Tech companies, healthcare systems, and remote-work migration have all added new demand to the housing market. In fact, Tulsa Remote — a program that pays remote workers $10,000 to relocate to the city — has attracted thousands of new residents since 2018, creating fresh rental and purchase demand that investors can tap into.

Home prices in Tulsa remain well below the national average, which is the core reason investors keep coming back. As of mid-2024, the median home price in Tulsa sits around $185,000 to $210,000, compared to the national median of roughly $420,000. Distressed properties and off-market deals can be acquired for as little as $60,000 to $90,000 in certain zip codes, leaving substantial room for profit on wholesale assignments, flips, and long-term rentals. Days on market average around 30 to 45 days for retail listings, but motivated seller properties and [off-market real estate deals](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/off-market-real-estate-deals) can close in as little as a week when you have the right buyer network in place.
Best Neighborhoods for Real Estate Investors in Tulsa

Not all of Tulsa is created equal from an investment standpoint. Understanding which neighborhoods offer the best returns — and which carry the most risk — is the difference between a profitable deal and an expensive mistake.
North Tulsa: High-Yield Rentals and Wholesale Opportunity

North Tulsa neighborhoods like Greenwood, Kendall-Whittier, and the broader 74106 and 74110 zip codes are heavily targeted by wholesalers and buy-and-hold investors. Properties here can be acquired for $50,000 to $100,000 and rented for $800 to $1,200 per month, producing gross rent multipliers and cap rates that are nearly impossible to find in coastal markets. The tradeoff is higher management intensity and slightly more vacancy risk, so factor those numbers carefully before committing.
Midtown Tulsa: The Fix-and-Flip Sweet Spot

Midtown neighborhoods including Cherry Street, Brookside, and the Pearl District have seen significant gentrification over the past decade. Older craftsman bungalows and ranch-style homes that need updating are common finds here. An investor can typically acquire a distressed property for $120,000 to $160,000, put $40,000 to $60,000 in renovations into it, and sell at an after-repair value of $260,000 to $320,000. That's a strong margin when you run the numbers through a deal analyzer. Use our free [ARV Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/arv-calculator) to quickly estimate your after-repair value before making any offer.
South Tulsa and Jenks: Stable Long-Term Rentals

South Tulsa — particularly areas near 71st Street and Yale, along with the neighboring suburb of Jenks — offers more stable, lower-risk rental properties. Homes here run $200,000 to $300,000, but they attract long-term tenants, experience low vacancy, and carry strong appreciation potential. These are ideal for investors building a portfolio of steady cash-flowing properties rather than chasing big wholesale assignment fees.
Types of Real Estate Deals Available in Tulsa
Wholesale Deals

Tulsa's affordable price points make it an excellent market for wholesaling. Assignment fees of $5,000 to $20,000 per deal are common, and the volume of distressed properties — particularly in North and East Tulsa — gives wholesalers consistent inventory to work with. Probate leads, tax-delinquent properties, and pre-foreclosure lists are especially productive in this market. For a full breakdown of the strategy, read our guide on [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners).
Fix-and-Flip Projects

Flippers love Tulsa for the same reason wholesalers do — low acquisition costs create wide profit margins. The city's housing stock skews older, with many homes built between the 1940s and 1980s that need modernization. Cosmetic flips in midtown can turn a $30,000 to $40,000 renovation budget into a $50,000 to $80,000 gross profit. The key is accurate ARV estimation and keeping a tight leash on your rehab budget. Experienced flippers typically target a minimum 20% net margin after all costs before pulling the trigger on a deal.
Buy-and-Hold Rentals

With a rental vacancy rate hovering around 7% and strong demand from the service industry, healthcare workers, and the growing remote-work population, Tulsa's rental market is healthy. Single-family homes in working-class neighborhoods can achieve the coveted 1% rule — where monthly rent equals or exceeds 1% of the purchase price — making positive cash flow achievable even with conservative financing assumptions.

Tulsa Real Estate Market Trends to Watch in 2024

items: Population growth driven by relocation incentives like Tulsa Remote is sustaining rental demand even as national markets cool.
Interest rate sensitivity: Higher rates have slowed retail buyer activity, which actually increases the motivated seller pool — a direct benefit for wholesalers and cash buyers.
Infrastructure investment: The city is investing heavily in its Gathering Place district and downtown core, which is pushing appreciation in adjacent neighborhoods.
Rising insurance costs in Oklahoma (partly due to storm risk) are squeezing margins for some landlords, so always budget $1,500 to $2,500 annually for homeowner's insurance on investment properties.

New construction in South Tulsa and Owasso is adding supply at the upper price points, which may cap appreciation for retail buyers above $300,000 but has little impact on the value-add investor segment.
Energy sector recovery is adding high-wage jobs back to the Tulsa economy, strengthening the buying pool for flipped properties in the $200,000 to $280,000 range.

Tips for Out-of-State Investors Targeting Tulsa

Tulsa is a market that rewards preparation. If you're investing from out of state, the learning curve is manageable — but only if you do it right. Before you [analyze your first real estate deal](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/how-to-analyze-real-estate-deals), make sure you understand how to read comparable sales, estimate rehab costs remotely, and build the right local team around you.

items: Build a local team first: Find a real estate agent who works with investors (not just retail buyers), a local general contractor you trust, and a property manager before you close your first deal.
Use virtual tools aggressively: Video walkthroughs, Google Street View, and AI-powered deal platforms let you underwrite deals without being on the ground for every inspection.

Focus on zip codes with data behind them: Stick to zip codes with proven rental histories and recent comparable sales until you know the market well. North Tulsa zip codes 74106 and 74110 and Midtown zip code 74114 are well-documented for investors.

Understand Oklahoma's landlord-tenant laws: Oklahoma is generally considered a landlord-friendly state, but eviction timelines and lease requirements still require attention — especially for out-of-state owners.

Join local real estate investor associations (REIAs): The Greater Tulsa Real Estate Investors Association hosts regular meetups and is an excellent source of buyer network contacts, contractors, and off-market deal flow.

Visit at least once before scaling: Even one trip to walk neighborhoods and meet your team in person dramatically reduces your risk and builds the local relationships that produce consistent deal flow.

Leverage technology for deal sourcing: AI-powered platforms can dramatically shorten the time it takes to identify motivated sellers and distressed properties in a new market — even from 1,000 miles away.

sections.content: Oklahoma has no state income tax on real estate gains for non-residents in the same way some states do, but consult a CPA familiar with Oklahoma tax law before making assumptions about your net returns. Property taxes in Tulsa County are low relative to the national average — typically 0.9% to 1.1% of assessed value — which is a meaningful advantage for buy-and-hold investors calculating long-term cash flow. Is Tulsa the Right Market for You?

Tulsa checks a lot of boxes that experienced investors look for: affordable entry points, diverse deal types, a growing population base, and a local economy that continues to mature and diversify. It's not a flashy market, and that's exactly the point. The best returns in real estate often come from markets where the numbers work — not from markets where everyone is competing over the same overpriced properties. If your goal is to build real wealth through real estate rather than just talk about it, Tulsa deserves a serious place in your investment strategy.
